title: Shelling Sarajevo: The SRK Campaign Against Civilians
sources: ICTY Galic Trial Judgment (IT-98-29-T), shelling incidents
content:
Throughout 1993, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps of the VRS conducted a sustained campaign of artillery and mortar fire against the civilian population of Sarajevo. From positions on the hills encircling the city, SRK forces directed fire into residential neighborhoods, marketplaces, water collection points, and other areas where civilians gathered in the course of daily life. The shelling was not a byproduct of combat between opposing military forces — it was a deliberate instrument of terror aimed at the civilian population of a besieged capital.

The ICTY Galić Trial Judgment (IT-98-29-T) examined this campaign in exhaustive detail. General Stanislav Galić commanded the SRK from September 1992 to August 1994, a period during which the corps maintained an artillery siege that the Trial Chamber found constituted a systematic attack on the civilian population. The judgment documented numerous specific shelling incidents, establishing through crater analysis, witness testimony, and ballistic evidence that the fire originated from SRK positions and struck locations with no legitimate military targets.

Among the incidents examined were shellings of queues at water distribution points, funeral gatherings, and residential areas. The pattern was consistent: mortar rounds and artillery shells struck at times and places calculated to inflict maximum civilian casualties. The city's residents adapted as best they could, sprinting across exposed intersections marked as sniper alleys, limiting movement during daylight, and retreating to basements during the heaviest bombardments. But adaptation could not eliminate the risk. The randomness of the shelling — any street, any hour — was itself part of its terrorizing effect.

The Trial Chamber convicted Galić of acts of violence the primary purpose of which was to spread terror among the civilian population, a violation of the laws and customs of war. The judgment was notable for its finding that terror against civilians constituted a distinct criminal offense under international humanitarian law. Galić was sentenced to life imprisonment on appeal.

The subsequent trial of General Dragomir Milošević (IT-98-29/1-T), who succeeded Galić as SRK commander in August 1994, established continuity in the campaign. The shelling and sniping did not abate with the change of command — the methods, the targets, and the intent remained consistent. Milošević was convicted on the same legal basis and sentenced to thirty-three years' imprisonment at trial, reduced to twenty-nine years on appeal.

The Bosnian Serb leadership maintained that the SRK's fire was directed at legitimate military targets and that the ARBiH bore responsibility for placing military assets among civilian areas. The ICTY examined and rejected this defense in both cases, finding that the proportion of fire directed at areas with no military significance was incompatible with any claim of lawful military operations.

For the population of Sarajevo, the shelling of 1993 represented the most intense phase of a siege that would ultimately last nearly four years. During peak periods, the city endured sustained bombardment with hundreds of shell impacts daily. The cumulative toll — in lives lost, bodies maimed, and psychological trauma inflicted — made the siege of Sarajevo one of the defining atrocities of the war. The city endured, but the cost of endurance was borne disproportionately by civilians who had no means of escape and no adequate shelter from the bombardment that defined their daily existence.
